issues.legal_issue: A property resumption carried out by an agent of a new sovereign during an unfinished acquisition of territory, against a resident who remains an alien and without purporting to act under ordinary law, is an act of State that municipal courts cannot review.
material_facts: After paramountcy lapsed, the former ruler was sovereign, but the territory had not acceded to the new Dominion; the ruler left the territory.
At the request of the former ruler’s council, the Dominion assumed the territory’s administration, and its Administrator acted as the Dominion’s agent.
The new sovereign had not formally completed the acquisition when the Administrator ordered the resumption of the property.
The property claimant was a resident of the territory and remained an alien to the new sovereign at the time of the order.

The Administrator cancelled the earlier grant and ordered the property resumed as State property; the order was not shown to have been made under law recognized by the new sovereign. The claimant sued for a declaration that the order was illegal.
issues.conclusion: The resumption was an act of State on behalf of the new sovereign and was not justiciable in municipal courts. The appeal was allowed and the suit dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: An act of State is an exercise of sovereign power against an alien that is neither grounded in nor purports to be grounded in municipal law. The test is whether the sovereign or its agent purported to act catastrophically, outside the ordinary course of law, or instead under legal authority. During the continuous process of acquiring territory, residents remain subjects of the former sovereign until the new sovereign assumes de jure sovereignty; their former rights do not bind the new sovereign unless it recognizes them. Retaining local laws does not, by itself, make the new sovereign subject to those laws. The Court relied on section 7 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, and on Salaman v. Secretary of State for India, Johnstone v. Pedlar, Secretary of State in Council for India v. Kamachee Boye Sahaba, Vaje Singh Ji Joravar Singh v. Secretary of State for India, and Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. v. Commissioner of Income-tax. It also considered Forester v. Secretary of State for India and referred to Campbell v. Hall, Ruding v. Smith, and East India Company v. Syed Ali.

rule.if: property_resumption_suit and new_sovereign_taking_over_foreign_territory and territorial_acquisition_incomplete and claimant_alien_at_time and sovereign_agent_ordered_resumption and action_outside_ordinary_law

predicates.property_resumption_suit: A claimant brought a suit challenging the resumption of property by a governmental authority.
predicates.new_sovereign_taking_over_foreign_territ: A new sovereign assumed the administration of territory that had previously been under another sovereign.
predicates.territorial_acquisition_incomplete: The new sovereign had not yet completed its assumption of de jure sovereignty over the territory.
predicates.claimant_alien_at_time: The claimant remained an alien to the new sovereign when the challenged action was taken.
predicates.sovereign_agent_ordered_resumption: An agent acting for the new sovereign ordered the property to be resumed.
predicates.action_outside_ordinary_law: The agent acted as an exercise of sovereign power and did not purport to act under the ordinary law governing the property.

issues.definition: When a property-resumption suit challenges an agent’s extra-legal sovereign action against an alien during an unfinished territorial takeover, the challenge is not justiciable.
